item.title: Resting-State Imaging of Vestibular Migraine:Integrative Insights from Amplitude,Homogeneity,and Functional Connection.
item.description:
Zhongguo yi xue ke xue yuan xue bao. Acta Academiae Medicinae Sinicae
Vestibular migraine (VM) represents a prevalent central vestibular disorder characterized by episodic vertigo and migraine attacks,yet its neuropathological basis remains poorly understood.Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging has emerged as a valuable investigative tool for identifying central network dysfunction in VM,given its sensitivity in detecting spontaneous brain activity.Drawing on seed-based functional connectivity studies and measures including amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations,fractional amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations,and regional homogeneity,this review examines aberrant spontaneous activity in VM patients across the thalamus,cerebellum,frontoparietal cortex,and insula.Key pathological circuits include disrupted vestibular-thalamo-cortical projections,dysregulated pain-emotion processing networks,and compensatory recruitment of visual-spatial attention and motor pathways.These findings furnish important neuroimaging evidence for understanding the pathophysiology and identifying the potential diagnostic and therapeutic biomarkers for VM.

item.title: Development of subcortical nuclei volume in utero over the second and third trimester.
item.description:
Brain imaging and behavior
Subcortical nuclei are important structures in the brain. Previous MRI evaluation of fetal brain development mostly focused on cerebral cortex and the myelination process, but few of them explored the developmental pattern of subcortical nuclei. The aim of this study is to analyze the developmental characteristics of fetal subcortical nuclei and their relationship with gestational age and cortical development. In this retrospective study, the precise axial, sagittal, and coronal views of T2-weighted brain MRI sequences in 47 fetuses with normal brains in the gestational age (GA) range of 22 to 36 weeks were obtained. A single 3D motion-corrected high-resolution brain volume was reconstructed from the 2D SSTSE imaging stacks using a slice-to-volume reconstruction (SVR) method. The volumes of the subcortical nuclei, i.e., amygdala, caudate, pallidum, putamen, hippocampus, subthalamic nucleus, thalamus, and cortex were segmented and corrected based on the above 3D images. We drew the developmental curve of each subcortical nucleus with age. The Pearson correlation coefficients were calculated between volumes of subcortical nuclei, as well as between volumes of cortical and subcortical regions, to explore how cortical regions and subcortical nuclei matured cooperatively. We illustrated the developmental trajectory curves of volumes of six subcortical nuclei and one of subcortical structure (thalamus, amygdala, hippocampus, caudate, putamen, subthalamic nucleus, and pallidum) according to the changes in GA to show the development trajectory of subcortical nuclei at 22-36 weeks. We further illustrated that volumes of subcortical nuclei and subcortical structure increased nonlinearly with GA, and the velopmental trajectories indicated laterality in the subcortical nuclei of the fetal brain. In addition, we found insignificant maturational coupling between subcortical nuclei and cortical regions, whereas the degree of maturational coupling between subcortical nuclei was relatively high. We found the volume of subcortical nuclei increased nonlinearly with the increase of GA, and the trajectory of nuclear mass development was lateral. The patterns of nuclear cluster development could expand our understanding of the brain growth. Reference ranges of fetal intracranial structures across gestational ages can serve as a valuable adjunct to prenatal counseling when interpreted in conjunction with clinical context and ultrasound findings.

item.title: Influence of regional white matter lesion volume differences related to cardiorespiratory fitness on cognition in healthy older adults.
item.description:
GeroScience
Greater cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF) has been associated with reduced global burden of white matter hyperintensity (WMH) lesions, a neuroimaging marker of small vessel cerebrovascular disease, and lower risk of age-related cognitive impairment and dementia. However, little is known about how CRF relates to regional patterns of WMH volume and the associated impact on cognitive aging. In a cohort of 166 community-dwelling, healthy older adults (mean age = 70.49 ± 9.96 years, 48.8% women), we investigated the association of CRF with regionally distributed WMH burden using multivariate regional network analysis of hemispheric lobar WMH volumes. We additionally evaluated the moderating role of CRF-related regional WMH volumetric differences for cognition. Higher CRF, distinct from self-reported habitual physical activity, was associated with a distributed covariance pattern of WMH volume reductions in bilateral frontal and right parietal lobes, with relative increases in bilateral occipital lobes. Greater CRF-WMH pattern expression was associated with younger age and male sex. Additionally, there was a significant age-by-CRF-WMH network pattern interaction for memory, but not for information processing speed and executive functioning, such that the higher the pattern expression, the weaker the inverse association between age and memory performance. Our findings suggest that having greater CRF may help to maintain cerebrovascular health in older adults as reflected in its association with reduced WMH burden in regions particularly vulnerable to brain aging and associated memory dysfunction. Multivariate CRF-WMH pattern expression may provide a marker of cerebrovascular health that may help to identify those at increased risk for age-related cognitive impairment.

item.title: Whole-Brain Dynamics and Cognitive Flexibility in Level 1 ASD: An HMM-Based Approach.
item.description:
Journal of autism and developmental disorders
PURPOSE: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a complex neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by differences in cognitive flexibility, which are closely associated with restricted and repetitive behaviors (RRB). However, the dynamic brain network mechanisms underlying these differences remain poorly understood. This study investigated the neural correlates of cognitive flexibility difficulties in ASD by analyzing dynamic brain network features and explored their potential as diagnostic biomarkers. METHODS: We applied hidden Markov models (HMMs) to resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) data to characterize dynamic brain network states in children with ASD (n = 69) and typically developing (TD) children (n = 50). Cognitive flexibility was assessed using the Behavior Rating Inventory of Executive Function (BRIEF). An independent ABIDE II dataset was used for external validation. Machine learning models evaluated the diagnostic utility of behavioral and neuroimaging markers. RESULTS: Children with ASD showed atypical brain network dynamics, specifically a reduced brain state switching rate (p < 0.01) and asymmetric activation of the frontoparietal network (FPN). These alterations were significantly associated with cognitive flexibility difficulties and RRB severity in the ASD group (Benjamini-Hochberg FDR q < 0.05) and generalized to the independent sample. Combining cognitive flexibility scores with brain state switching rates yielded high diagnostic accuracy (internal AUC: 0.897 (95% CI 0.812-0.963); external AUC: 0.869 (95% CI 0.781-0.943)). CONCLUSION: This study provides novel insights into the dynamic neural mechanisms underlying cognitive flexibility differences in ASD. The findings support combined behavioral and neuroimaging biomarkers for improving ASD diagnosis and lay the groundwork for individualized intervention research.

item.title: Network Control Theory in Psychiatry: From Connectivity-Derived Controllability to Brain-State Transitions and Interventions.
item.description:
Neuroscience and biobehavioral reviews
Psychiatric disorders are increasingly conceptualized as disruptions in brain dynamics, particularly in how activity patterns evolve over time. Network Control Theory (NCT), a framework derived from control engineering, has emerged as a promising approach for studying these dynamics. Yet, despite its growing application in psychiatry, it remains unclear whether NCT has provided mechanistic or clinical insights beyond conventional measures of network topology. Here, we conducted a PRISMA-guided systematic review of NCT applications across major psychiatric disorders in adults. Of 178 records identified, 26 studies met inclusion criteria, representing 17 unique cohorts spanning schizophrenia spectrum disorders, major depressive disorder, bipolar disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and post-traumatic stress disorder. Across studies, a recurring pattern of lower modal controllability was reported in several disorders (3 independent cohorts), although regional findings were heterogeneous and diagnostic specificity was limited. In contrast, task-based analyses under cognitive load (2 cohorts) and energy-based metrics (2 cohorts), though scarce, revealed more extensive case-control abnormalities and between-disorder differentiation. Intervention studies provided preliminary evidence that NCT-derived measures may predict treatment response and inform individualized neuromodulation targets (4 cohorts). However, 21 of 26 studies exclusively relied on connectivity-derived controllability metrics that were closely related to conventional measures of network topology and characterized model-implied control properties rather than directly observed state transitions. Furthermore, translational evidence came largely from single-arm, retrospective and simulation studies. The distinct value of NCT in psychiatry therefore remains to be established. Future progress requires the use of empirically observed brain states, energy-based measures, and prospective intervention studies.

item.title: Combined Neuromelanin-Sensitive and Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging Links Midbrain Dopaminergic Dysfunction to Connectome Architecture in First-Episode, Medication-Naïve Major Depressive Disorder.
item.description:
Biological psychiatry
Accumulating evidence implicates dopaminergic dysfunction in major depressive disorder (MDD), yet direct evidence of such dysfunction and of its altered coupling with the functional connectome remains limited. Using neuromelanin-sensitive MRI (NM-MRI) and resting-state fMRI, we examined differences in substantia nigra/ventral tegmental area NM-MRI signal (NMSSN/VTA) between first-episode, medication-naïve MDD patients (n = 112) and healthy controls (HC; n = 230). Network-based statistics (NBS) assessed MDD-related alterations in NMSSN/VTA-functional connectivity (FC) coupling. Spatial correspondence analyses examined the spatial convergence of these coupling alterations with normative dopaminergic molecular maps and anhedonia-related connectome patterns in MDD. Patients with MDD showed lower NMSSN/VTA, with more pronounced reductions in lateral and rostral regions. NBS identified a widespread component with altered NMSSN/VTA-FC coupling in MDD, characterized predominantly by higher slopes across attention, control, sensory, and medial temporal systems and lower slopes involving limbic-striatal and default-mode connections. Network-level analysis further identified a diagnosis-dependent NMSSN/VTA-striatal-limbic connectivity relationship, with lower NMSSN/VTA associated with higher FC in MDD. Spatially, these coupling alterations converged with dopaminergic molecular architecture, showing negative correspondence with normative dopaminergic receptor and transporter distributions and positive correspondence with the anticipatory-pleasure-related connectome pattern in MDD. These findings provide in vivo evidence of midbrain dopaminergic dysfunction and widespread disruption of dopaminergic-connectome coupling in MDD, with these coupling alterations spatially converging with anhedonia-related connectome organization. Together, these findings advance our understanding of the role of dopaminergic dysfunction in the pathophysiology of MDD.

item.title: Occupational overwork is associated with regional cortical gray-to-white matter signal ratio.
item.description:
International archives of occupational and environmental health
Occupational overwork has been associated with cognitive dysfunction and increased vulnerability to neurodegenerative processes. However, the exact neurostructural alterations underlying overwork remain insufficiently characterized. This study aimed to investigate whether prolonged working hours are associated with cortical microstructural changes using the gray-to-white matter signal intensity ratio (GWR), a non-invasive MRI-based marker of cortical integrity, to better understand the neurological risks of overwork. A cross-sectional MRI analysis was conducted in 110 participants (32 overworked, > 52 h/week; 78 non-overworked, ≤ 52 h/week). 3D T1-weighted images were acquired at 3.0 T MRI and GWR was computed using FreeSurfer surface-based analysis by sampling gray and white matter signal intensities along cortical surfaces. Group differences were assessed using vertex-wise general linear models (GLM) adjusted for age, sex, and education level followed by cluster-wise Monte Carlo simulations for multiple comparison correction. Associations of regional GWR with continuous weekly working hours and regional white-matter fractional anisotropy (FA) were examined as exploratory supplementary observations, with false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Seven right-hemisphere clusters showed significant group differences in GWR (cluster-wise corrected p < 0.05). GWR was higher in the overwork group in the precentral, postcentral, supramarginal, and middle temporal cortices, but lower in the superior frontal cortex. Exploratory analyses in these same-sample selected clusters showed associations with weekly working hours in directions consistent with the group differences (FDR corrected p ≤ 0.004). GWR in the right precentral and supramarginal clusters was negatively associated with regional white-matter FA (FDR corrected p < 0.05). Chronic occupational overwork was associated with regional GWR alterations. These findings suggest that GWR may serve as a non-invasive imaging marker for detecting brain changes related to prolonged working hours, highlighting the need for further investigation into the impact of occupational factors on brain health.

item.title: The relationship between socio-environmental factors, brain growth and cognition in middle childhood.
item.description:
Pediatric research
The relationship between socio-environmental factors, brain growth, and cognition in childhood is unknown. This study aimed to characterize associations between (i) regional brain growth from birth to 6-8 years and socio-environmental factors; and (ii) regional brain growth and cognitive outcomes in middle childhood. One hundred and thirty-seven 6-8-year-old children (25 with congenital heart disease) underwent neonatal and paediatric brain MRI and a full-scale IQ assessment. Data on household income, maternal education, neighborhood deprivation, and early cognitively stimulating home environment were collected. Regional brain growth (extracerebral CSF, ventricles, cortical grey matter, white matter, deep grey matter, cerebellum, brainstem) from the neonatal period to 6-8 years was assessed using Gaussian process regression. Low household income was associated with reduced cortical grey matter growth (B, 95% CI -1.14, -1.88 to -0.396; pFWE = 0.044) and extracerebral CSF expansion (-1.55, -2.51 to -0.585; pFWE = 0.042). Higher cortical grey matter (3.89, 1.12-6.65; pFWE = 0.038) and brainstem (3.24, 0.894-5.58; pFWE = 0.038) growth were associated with better full-scale IQ. Brainstem (p = 0.014), but not cortical grey matter (p = 0.177), remained significant after adjustment for socio-environmental factors. Support for financially vulnerable families may promote brain growth. Brainstem growth is a brain correlate of childhood cognition independent of the effects of socio-environmental factors. One hundred and thirty-seven children (25 with congenital heart disease) underwent neuroimaging at birth and at 6-8 years and a full-scale IQ assessment at 6-8 years. Household income, maternal education, neighborhood deprivation and early home environment data were collected. After adjustment for other socio-environmental factors and group, low household income was associated with reduced cortical grey matter growth and extracerebral CSF expansion. Higher cortical grey matter and brainstem growth were associated with higher full-scale IQ in middle childhood. Household poverty was linked to reduced brain growth, while cortical grey matter and brainstem growth were associated with cognitive abilities in childhood.

item.title: Spatial Heterogeneity of Brain Myelin Aging and Vascular-Metabolic Risk-Associated Alterations: An MR Fingerprinting Study.
item.description:
NeuroImage
To characterize spatial patterns of age-related variation in MR fingerprinting (MRF)-derived myelin water fraction (MWF) and its associations with vascular-metabolic risk. In this cross-sectional study, neurologically asymptomatic adults underwent MRF scanning at 3T MR. MWF maps were estimated using a three-compartment model. Non-negative matrix factorization identified cortical gray matter (GM) and white matter (WM) clusters in healthy participants; eight subcortical regions were analyzed separately. Generalized additive models were used to generate healthy reference curves. Deviations, aging slopes, and exposure-by-age interactions were compared between healthy controls and participants with vascular-metabolic risk. Among 285 participants (57.2 ± 14.4 years; 168 females), 167 were healthy and 118 had vascular-metabolic risk. Two cortical GM and two WM clusters with distinct aging patterns were identified. GM cluster 2 (frontal-parietal-occipital cortices) showed higher MWF with age, and WM cluster 2 (projection and association fibers) showed marked negative age association after midlife. Compared with healthy participants, the vascular-metabolic risk group had a less positive age association in GM clusters (cluster 1: β = -2.77 × 10-5/year, q = 0.046; cluster 2: β = -4.14 × 10-5/year, q = 0.034) and lower deviation from the healthy reference in WM cluster 2 (β = -0.00351, q = 0.036). Continuous blood-pressure main effects on deviation were nonsignificant after FDR correction, but complementary tertile analyses showed more negative age-related slopes in the highest than the lowest tertiles in WM cluster 2 and the subcortical summary (all FDR-corrected q < 0.01). MRF-derived MWF imaging revealed regionally distinct myelin aging patterns and selective deviations linked to vascular-metabolic risk, particularly in projection and association WM fibers. Blood pressure may be relevant to regional myelin-related aging patterns, warranting validation in larger longitudinal cohorts.

item.title: Motor pre-selection modulates action observation effects in sensorimotor cortices: a MEG study.
item.description:
NeuroImage
According to the Motor Simulation theory, observing an action automatically activates matching motor representations. This can explain why, in automatic imitation tasks, responses are faster when the observed action matches the required one, compared to when it differs. However, the automatic imitation task setting represents a very peculiar situation where participants need to pre-select the motor representations corresponding to the actions that they might observe, a situation quite different from daily-life contexts such as sports (e.g., tennis or basketball) where actions pre-selected for output are typically different from those observed, and where imitation errors or tendencies are seldom observed. This leads to the following question: Does the motor cortex response to observed actions depend on whether they match the motor representations pre-selected for output? In the present magnetoencephalography experiment, we studied, within the hand-related primary sensorimotor cortex, the oscillatory dynamics produced by the observation of hand actions in two conditions: either while participants pre-selected motor representations similar to those observed, or while they pre-selected markedly different motor representations, such as those involved in feet actions. Our data show that the motor cortex reacts differently to action observation in the two pre-selection conditions: alpha- and beta-band activity showed stronger desynchronization when the pre-selection involved motor representations matching those observed compared to non-matching ones. Specifically, observing hand actions while pre-selecting non-matching feet movements elicited a late rebound-like increase in alpha- and beta-band activity that was not observed when hand actions were pre-selected.

item.title: Explainable multi-group dynamic causal distribution learning framework to disentangle common and specific dynamic effective connectivity across MCI stages.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Brain functional networks exhibit an intrinsic architecture that is preserved across brain disorder groups, upon which different groups display distinct patterns of abnormal interactions. Exploring the common and specific network patterns is crucial for revealing common pathological mechanisms, group-specific alterations, and disease progression. Dynamic effective connectivity (dEC) characterizes time-varying causal interactions among brain regions and provides an effective means of investigating common and specific network patterns. However, the disentangled learning of common and specific dEC across multiple groups remains underexplored, limiting a systematic understanding of dynamic causal mechanisms in brain networks across disorders and disease stages. We propose an explainable multi-group dynamic causal distribution learning framework that integrates spatial and temporal information to identify common and specific dEC distributions among different groups. Experiments on synthetic datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework effectively and robustly identifies causality and disentangles common and specific causal structures. When applied to real-world data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, the proposed framework uncovers common and specific dEC across mild cognitive impairment (MCI) stages. Results show that, as MCI worsens, the dEC within the visual network and among functional hubs of the default mode network remain stable, whereas dEC associated with episodic memory, emotional processing, and interoception shift from compensatory to decompensatory patterns. The code is available at https://github.com/OrangeLY-byte/EMGDCD.

item.title: Long-term heading exposure in relation to structural MRI markers and neurocognitive function in retired professional soccer players.
item.description:
Journal of neuroradiology = Journal de neuroradiologie
Repetitive head impacts from purposeful heading in soccer have raised concerns about long-term neurological effects, but in vivo MRI markers remain underexplored. Most published imaging studies have involved amateur, youth or currently active players. Retired professionals with a full career of heading exposure and no reported concussion have rarely been investigated. Our objective was to evaluate structural brain differences and neuropsychological performance in retired or late-career professional soccer players without concussion history compared to high-level athletes from non-contact sports. In this cross-sectional study, male professional soccer players and male non-contact athletes underwent 3T brain MRI and standardized cognitive testing. Imaging included volumetric assessment of the cavum septi pellucidi (CSP) and cavum vergae, automated quantification of white matter hyperintensities (WMH), voxel-based morphometry analysis of regional brain volume, and cerebral microbleed detection. Neuropsychological testing assessed reaction time, memory, attention, and executive functioning. Twenty-nine soccer players (mean age 44.5 years, SD 7.3) and 29 non-contact athletes (mean age 41.9 years, SD 8.0) were included. Players reported 29.7 years of practice, including 13.3 professionally, and 9.9 years since retirement. Soccer players demonstrated significantly greater CSP volume (21 vs 6 mm³; p < 0.001) and greater total WMH volume after age adjustment (3892 vs 2833 mm³; p = 0.046), mainly periventricular. Voxel-based morphometry showed reduced grey matter volume in the right anterior temporal lobe (p = 0.030, corrected), and in other frontotemporal regions and the head of the left caudate nucleus (p < 0.001, uncorrected). No microbleeds were detected in either group. Neuropsychological testing showed no cognitive impairment. Retired or late-career soccer players showed a pattern of subtle structural MRI differences from non-contact athletes consistent with that reported in populations exposed to repetitive head impacts, without measurable differences in neurocognitive performance.

item.title: Spatial Transcriptomics Reveals the Macroscale Signatures of Cortical Cell Types on Anatomic Magnetic Resonance Imaging.
item.description:

Gray/white matter contrast (GWC) of [Formula: see text]-weighted MRI is an abundantly available phenotype often used to investigate aging and cognition. Despite growing interest in investigating microstructure using GWC, its relationship to cell type-related tissue properties is understudied. We leverage spatially resolved post-mortem transcriptomic data from six donors to identify associations between cell type marker genes and GWC averaged across cognitively normal living adults ([Formula: see text] = 577, mean age = 56.2 years). Astrocyte marker gene transcription is significantly associated with cortical variation in mean GWC, referred to as [Formula: see text]. Additionally, estimated relative astrocyte abundance correlates significantly with [Formula: see text] ([Formula: see text] = 0.409, [Formula: see text] < 0.01). Gene transcription correlations with [Formula: see text] are enriched for oligodendrocyte marker genes only within the frontal lobe, which is known to age fastest. Transcriptions of genes related to iron trafficking and myelination help to identify potential explanations for associations of [Formula: see text] to astrocyte and oligodendrocyte distributions.
