item.title: Theory of mind, autism-like traits, executive functions, and structural brain MRI findings in children with neurofibromatosis type 1.
item.description:
European journal of pediatrics
This study aimed to examine social-cognitive difficulties in children with neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) by jointly investigating theory of mind (ToM), executive functions, and autism-like traits and to explore whether children with NF1 show structural differences in brain regions commonly implicated in social cognition and executive functioning. In this two-center cross-sectional study, 41 children aged 8-18 years were included, comprising 21 children with NF1 and 20 age- and sex-matched typically developing children. Participants underwent behavioral assessment, including parent-reported autism-like traits, everyday executive functioning, and direct measures of ToM. Structural brain MRI data were analyzed using automated volumetric and cortical thickness measures, focusing on these regions. Children with NF1 showed higher autism-like traits, lower everyday executive functioning in play and social routines, and poorer performance on an advanced ToM task. The NF1 group also had larger global brain volume reflecting widespread white matter expansion; lower cortical gray matter proportion and thickness in frontal, temporal, parietal, cingulate, and limbic regions; and larger subcortical structures including the amygdala, hippocampus, and thalamus. Exploratory within-group brain-behavior correlations were few and selective, none survived multiple-comparison correction, and none involved autism-like traits. Children with NF1 display a multidimensional profile of social-cognitive difficulties together with structural differences indicating an imbalance between cortical and subcortical regions typically involved in social cognition. These structural differences offer a possible neurobiological substrate for the social-cognitive difficulties observed in NF1. Whether they account for these difficulties remains to be tested in samples powered to examine brain-behavior associations directly. • Children with neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) frequently show executive dysfunction, autism-like traits, and theory of mind (ToM) difficulties. • These domains have rarely been examined jointly, or alongside brain structure, in the same children. • Autism-like traits, everyday executive difficulties, and poorer ToM co-occurred in children with NF1. • The same children showed reduced cortical thickness and proportion with enlarged subcortical structures in regions implicated in social cognition, a candidate substrate for future brain-behavior studies.

item.title: Cognitive control networks in human and macaque.
item.description:
eLife
A much-replicated finding in human brain imaging is a distributed 'multiple-demand' or MD system, increasing in activity for many kinds of cognitive demand, and centrally involved in cognitive control. MD regions are proposed to encode a distributed mental model of critical task events, bound together in the roles and relationships needed to direct action selection. Though previous data hint at a corresponding network in the macaque, there has been no direct comparison to human data. Here we used functional magnetic resonance imaging to measure whole-brain activation in a multi-step saccadic maze task, compared to a control requiring similar moves but without goal-based decisions. Human data were a close match to the canonical MD network, extended to include adjacent regions, and in particular much of the canonical dorsal attention network. Data from two monkeys suggested correspondences in dorsomedial frontal, insula/orbitofrontal, and posterior temporal cortex. In lateral frontal cortex, there was just a single, largely dorsal activation patch, in contrast to multiple distinct human patches. In one animal, as in humans, there was accompanying activation of dorsal and medial parietal cortex. In macaques, as in humans, together with previous data, our findings suggest an extended and strongly interconnected brain network recruited by increased cognitive challenge.

item.title: Ramping-up hippocampal ripples and their neocortical coupling support human visual short-term memory.
item.description:
eLife
Emerging evidence suggests that the hippocampus contributes to visual short-term memory (VSTM). However, the neural mechanisms through which hippocampal activity supports the maintenance of VSTM representations remain largely unknown. Here, using intracranial EEG recordings from human participants performing a delayed match-to-sample task for naturalistic objects, we investigated the role of hippocampal ripple activity-brief high-frequency oscillations associated with memory replay-in VSTM maintenance and hippocampal-neocortical communication. We found that hippocampal ripple rates progressively ramped up during the maintenance period and supported successful VSTM. More critically, hippocampal ripples were temporally coupled with the ripples in the lateral temporal lobe (LTL), and these coupled ripples were associated with memory reactivation in the LTL. These findings provide direct evidence that hippocampal-neocortical interaction via coupled ripples supports VSTM, extending the role of hippocampal ripples from long-term consolidation to short-term mnemonic processes and offering new insights into the dynamic coding mechanisms of working memory.

item.title: Functional and structural neuroplasticity of motor system in hemiplegic cerebral palsy
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Hemiplegic cerebral palsy results from a unilateral prenatal or perinatal brain injury and causes motor impairments in the contralateral side of the body. Variable functional outcomes among children with hemiplegic cerebral palsy despite similar lesion extent suggest that developmental neuroplasticity and brain reorganization contribute to motor function. By using multimodal neuroimaging, we characterize the structural and functional reorganization of the motor system and examine its associations with lesion characteristics and upper-limb performance. We examined 26 children with hemiplegic cerebral palsy and 26 typically developing controls using electromagnetic source imaging to map the primary motor cortex and characterize movement-related oscillations across physiologically relevant frequency bands, navigated transcranial magnetic stimulation to assess motor cortical excitability and lateralization, and functionally guided diffusion-weighted MRI to evaluate the structural integrity of descending motor and motor commissural fibers. We further assessed upper-limb function using Melbourne Assessment 2 and examined multimodal relationships using correlation, cross-validated latent-variable, and mediation analyses. Children with hemiplegic cerebral palsy showed microstructural abnormalities in the descending motor and motor commissural fibers, characterized by lower fractional anisotropy and higher mean, axial, and radial diffusivity (all P < 0.05). The navigated transcranial magnetic stimulation identified ipsilateral corticospinal projections from the less affected hemisphere in 17 of 22 children (77%) with hemiplegic cerebral palsy, accompanied by reduced contralesional primary motor cortex lateralization (P < 0.05). The hemiplegic cerebral palsy group also exhibited hemisphere-specific abnormalities in movement-related oscillations, including reduced theta synchronization in the contralesional hemisphere and attenuated mu- and beta-band desynchronization in the ipsilesional hemisphere (all P < 0.05). Larger lesions were associated with poorer motor performance (Rho = -0.74 to -0.57, P < 0.05). Reduced descending motor fiber integrity was associated with impaired dexterity and attenuated mu- and beta-band desynchronization (Rho = -0.51 to 0.62, P < 0.05), while motor commissural fiber integrity was associated with corticospinal motor lateralization (Rho = -0.45 to 0.41, P < 0.05). A cross-validated multimodal structural-functional model predicted motor function (Q^2 = 0.42, P < 0.001) more accurately than structural measures alone (Q^2 = 0.25). Beta-band desynchronization mediated the association between descending motor fiber integrity and motor performance (indirect effect = 0.12 SD, 95% CI 0.03-0.24). Developmental motor neuroplasticity in hemiplegic cerebral palsy reflects an integrated structure-physiology-behavior process rather than the direct consequence of lesion burden alone. Multimodal biomarkers may improve prognostication and support individualized rehabilitation and neuromodulation.

item.title: What's in a Story? Studying Neural Narrative Engagement with Auditory Passages Using EEG Inter-Subject Correlation
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Narrative engagement - a state implicating attention as well as emotional and sequential processing - is crucial in contexts ranging from social interaction to education. Yet we still lack an understanding of how narrative contents and listener perceptions relate to the neural responses they elicit. In this study, we investigate relationships between auditory narratives and listener responses using electroencephalography inter-subject correlation (EEG-ISC), a measure of neural synchrony that has been shown to correlate with narrative cohesion, attention, preference, and learning. We analyzed dense-array EEG recorded from 46 adult participants who listened to social and non-social narrated literary excerpts. The data were spatially optimized using Reliable Components Analysis, and ISC was calculated for each of the three maximally reliable components (RCs) on a per-stimulus basis. While we found no significant relationships between EEG-ISC and broad social/non-social categorizations of the excerpts, ISC for high sociocognitive word usage significantly exceeded that of medium and low word usage in the third spatial component, RC3. We further observed a significant positive correlation between participants' summed ratings of interest, compulsion, and enjoyment and ISC, both for RC2 and when summed across RC1-RC3. Interaction analyses suggest that passage content and behavioral responses contributed independently as additive effects to these relationships. Taken together, these findings extend previous research utilizing EEG-ISC in natural speech contexts and, importantly, suggest that the decomposition of EEG into maximally correlated spatial components can separate co-occurring neural processes engaged during story listening.

item.title: Neural competition predicts speech production advantages in congenital amusia
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Mental health research has traditionally been deficit-focused, and cognitive advantages in mental conditions have almost always been documented retrospectively. Here we propose and test an a priori pathway for predicting such advantages from a condition's impaired neural basis, neural competition and brain-mind associations. Using congenital amusia (CA), a neurodevelopmental disorder with a well-defined deficit in right frontotemporal circuit (FTC), as a model, we predicted that interhemispheric competition would release the left homologue from inhibition, conferring advantages in speech production. Two independent studies, multimodal neuroimaging and behavioral testing, confirmed this prediction: MRI revealed right FTC impairment alongside competitive-like benefits of the left FTC in CA; and CA showed speech production advantages with intact episodic memory and constrained music learning. These findings provide the first empirical demonstration that cognitive advantages can be predicted in advance and then verified, offering a principled, mechanism-based alternative to the deficit-focused paradigm.

item.title: Microstructure predicts cognition following deep brain stimulation in Parkinson's disease
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Deep brain stimulation of the subthalamic nucleus (STN-DBS) effectively treats motor and non-motor symptoms in advanced Parkinson's disease (PD). However, 15-20 % of patients experience postoperative cognitive decline and identifying preoperative markers remains an unmet clinical need. In this prospective open-label study, we employed NODDI-DTI to investigate whether cerebral microstructure predicts cognitive outcomes following STN-DBS. Forty PD patients underwent diffusion MRI and neuropsychological assessments at preoperative baseline and 6-month follow-up. A whole-brain voxel-wise analysis related microstructural metrics to postoperative cognitive change. Compromised microstructure within three large-scale networks - the frontoparietal/attentional, default mode/limbic, and ventral associative/visual networks - was associated with greater postoperative cognitive decline. These findings suggest that both disease-related network degeneration and stimulation acting on compromised circuits may contribute to postoperative cognitive decline. In conclusion, preoperative evaluation of microstructural integrity may help identify patients at risk for postoperative cognitive decline, supporting individualised counselling and targeted behavioural monitoring after STN-DBS.

item.title: Diffusion-based vertex-wise connectomics encodes individual differences in cognition, affect and pathology
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
No two brains are wired alike, and much of a person's cognitive and clinical state is written in this individual variation, not in the group average. Structural connectomes, however, are typically read through group atlases that summarize connectivity into regional averages, leaving this individual signal untapped. We build a vertex-wise structural connectome, in which every cortical surface vertex is a node, and apply it across the Alzheimer's continuum. Using an independent dataset for methodological development and a multisite cohort of 317 participants from ADNI-4, we show that connection distance and organizational scale form a nested hierarchy, from a long-range backbone to fine, short-range structure. The individual fingerprint is strongest in medium- and short-range connections and becomes less distinctive as connectivity is pooled into atlas parcels. This individual structure can be recovered across spatial scales, although its fidelity depends on diffusion acquisition quality, with multishell data providing a more informative reference than single-shell data. In the aging brain, an individually referenced balance between short- and long-range connectivity is associated with episodic memory, cognitive reserve, depressive symptoms, and shared molecular pathology. While cognitive associations largely reflect diagnostic differences, associations with depressive symptoms and pathology burden remain detectable after adjustment for diagnosis. These findings show that individual structural connectomes retain clinically and biologically relevant variation that is not fully captured by diagnostic classification or group-level summaries.

item.title: Discourse coherence in first-episode psychosis and depression: shared referential alterations and links to cortical hierarchy
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Disrupted discourse coherence is documented in psychosis, but whether depression shows similar alterations, and how these relate to cortical hierarchical organization, remains unclear. This is the first study to examine conceptual and referential dimensions of coherence and their associations with cortical hierarchy across first-episode psychosis and depression. We analysed spontaneous speech from 85 German speakers (29 controls, 28 with first-episode psychosis, 28 with first-episode depression), of whom 80 underwent resting-state fMRI. Using large-model embeddings, automated coreference resolution, and graph-theoretical measures, we quantified conceptual relations (i.e., how ideas are linked) and referential relations (i.e., how entities are introduced and maintained), and related them to gradient dispersion between networks and within the semantic-associative network. Both clinical groups showed reduced referential continuity, and less small-world organization of conceptual content than controls, whereas differences in local semantic similarity depended on diagnosis and language model. Negative symptom severity was associated with altered conceptual and referential relations. Between-network gradient dispersion did not differ between groups. However, after controlling for diagnosis, individual variation in gradient organization was associated with distinct conceptual and referential relations. Visual-default mode network dispersion was associated with conceptual network organization, while somatomotor-default mode network dispersion was associated with local conceptual and referential coherence. Dispersion within the semantic-associative network was linked with topic reorganization. These findings identify reduced referential continuity as a shared, automatically measurable speech alteration across early psychosis and depression, linked to negative symptoms and cortical hierarchy, and support developing scalable speech-based markers for transdiagnostic assessment and differential diagnosis.

item.title: Genetic, metabolic and hippocampal myelin contributions to episodic memory ageing
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract There is ongoing controversy about the role of the apolipoprotein-E (APOE) genotype in modulating cognitive trajectories in healthy ageing and Alzheimer’s disease. We investigated associations between APOE genotype, cardiometabolic and inflammatory profiles, lifestyle, and hippocampal microstructure with late-life episodic memory trajectories in a community-dwelling, mid-to-old-age cohort. The genotyped sample (n = 5325) with follow-up spanning over 20 years included nested cognitive (n = 1378) and neuroimaging subsamples (n = 301). We first tested whether the APOE ε4 allele was associated with systemic physiological profiles across adulthood, followed by assessment of APOE associations with cognitive ageing trajectories and their relationships with health profiles and MRI markers of hippocampal myelination. APOE ε4 carrier status was associated with an adverse lipid-related metabolic profile across adulthood. In late-life, APOE ε4 was selectively associated with steeper age-related episodic memory decline across cognitive domains examined, with effects emerging in the eighth decade of life and evident already among heterozygous carriers. Individual metabolic, inflammatory, cardiovascular, and lifestyle markers did not account for this APOE ε4-related memory effect. When considered jointly within their respective domains, adverse metabolic burden was associated with poorer episodic memory performance and reduced odds of memory maintenance, whereas a favorable lifestyle profile was associated with better episodic memory function, independently of APOE genotype. The association between hippocampal myelin content and steepness of episodic memory trajectories was stronger in APOE ε4 carriers, while hippocampal volume showed only a trend. These findings indicate that APOE ε4 is primarily linked to episodic memory decline dynamics, with hippocampal myelin marking trajectory differences, whereas peripheral metabolic burden and lifestyle relates to memory performance level.

item.title: Connectome Harmonic Analysis at 7 Tesla Reveals Selective Reorganization of Large-Scale Cortical Dynamics in Adult Users of Cannabis.
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Background Cannabis exposure is associated with altered functional connectivity, cognitive impairment, and psychosis-spectrum risk, but the systems-level principles through which it reshapes large-scale brain organization remain poorly understood. Connectome Harmonic Analysis (CHA), a spectral graph-theoretic framework, characterizes the intrinsic spatial modes governing cortical communication. We investigated whether cannabis use alters low-frequency connectome harmonics using ultra-high-field 7 Tesla MRI. Methods Resting-state fMRI and high angular resolution diffusion data from the Human Connectome Project 7T cohort were used for Connectome Harmonic Analysis in 81 cannabis users (CU) and 81 matched non-users (NU). BOLD activity was projected onto the first 200 connectome harmonics; group differences in harmonic power were assessed with independent-samples t-tests and FDR correction, and significant harmonics were anatomically localized using the HCP multimodal parcellation atlas. Results Cannabis users exhibited significantly increased power in a single low-frequency connectome harmonic (k = 6; λ₆ = 0.01144; t ≈ 4.19; p_FDR = 7.21 × 10⁻³; Cohen’s d = 0.659), reflecting approximately 44% greater normalized power than non-users; no higher-frequency harmonics survived correction. This harmonic localized to a distributed frontoparietal–sensorimotor network spanning bilateral premotor, supplementary motor, and superior parietal cortex, intraparietal sulcus, and supramarginal gyrus, and did not correlate with cannabis clinical exposure variables (age at onset, duration, frequency, or abuse/dependence diagnosis; all ρ < 0.09, p > 0.44). Behavioral correlation analyses revealed nominal, domain-specific associations — slower working memory reaction time across the cohort (ρ = +0.18, p = 0.026), greater ADHD symptom burden (ρ = +0.23, p = 0.041) and extraversion (ρ = +0.25, p = 0.026) in cannabis users, and lower theory-of-mind accuracy in non-users (ρ = −0.23, p = 0.042) — though standard cognitive composites were null and no association survived FDR correction. Conclusions Cannabis use is associated with selective amplification of a low-frequency connectome harmonic subserving frontoparietal–sensorimotor integration, suggesting that cannabis exposure alters the brain’s intrinsic dynamical architecture at the level of macroscale eigenmodes rather than isolated regional circuits. Connectome harmonics may thus provide a systems-level biomarker linking cannabinoid neurobiology to cortical coordination relevant to psychosis vulnerability, predictive processing abnormalities, and network dysregulation in psychiatric illness.

item.title: Motor imagery-based brain-computer interface training for upper-limb rehabilitation after subacute stroke: A randomized sham-controlled trial.
item.description:
PloS one
Objective To determine whether motor imagery (MI) based brain-computer interface (BCI) training improves upper-limb motor function in patients with subacute stroke compared with a high-fidelity sham-BCI control, and to explore accompanying structural and resting-state functional MRI changes. Method In this participant-blinded randomized controlled trial, 32 patients with subacute stroke were randomized to a MI-based BCI group or a high-fidelity BCI sham-control group (n = 16 each). Both groups received dose-matched training (30 min/session, 5 sessions/week for 4 weeks) in addition to standard rehabilitation. Upper-limb motor outcomes were assessed using the Fugl-Meyer Assessment-Upper Extremity (FMA-UE; primary outcome), Wolf Motor Function Test (WMFT), Motor Assessment Scale (MAS), and Modified Barthel Index (MBI). Structural MRI and resting-state functional MRI were acquired at baseline and post-intervention to assess gray matter volume (GMV) and functional connectivity (FC). Results Both groups showed significant improvement after the intervention. Compared with the sham-control group, the MI-based BCI group demonstrated greater gains in FMA-UE and secondary motor outcomes (WMFT and MAS), whereas the difference in MBI was not statistically significant. Voxel-based morphometry revealed a within-group increase in GMV in the contralesional supplementary motor area (SMA) in the MI-based BCI group; however, no significant between-group GMV difference was observed. The MI-based BCI group also exhibited increased resting-state FC between the SMA and the ipsilesional cerebellar lobule IX and fusiform gyrus. Changes in FC were associated with improvements in FMA-UE, WMFT, and MBI, but not MAS. Conclusion Compared with a high-fidelity sham-control group, MI-based BCI group training was associated with greater upper-limb motor recovery in patients with subacute stroke, accompanied by changes in structural and functional neuroimaging measures involving motor-related regions and connections. Larger randomized controlled trials with longer follow-up are required to confirm durability and clinical relevance. Trial registration Chinese Clinical Trial Registry ChiCTR2100052452.

item.title: Balance dısorders and structural and connectıvıty changes in the cerebellum in bıpolar dısorder: A dıffusıon tensor imagıng study.
item.description:
The neuroradiology journal
The aim of this study was to evaluate balance performance in individuals with bipolar disorder (BD) and to examine changes in white matter connections associated with cerebellar structures using cranial magnetic resonance (MR) imaging.The study included 30 BD patients and 25 healthy controls with available cranial MR images. Balance performance was assessed, and tractography analyses examined the pathways of the superior cerebellar peduncle (SCP), middle cerebellar peduncle (MCP), inferior cerebellar peduncle (ICP), medial lemniscus (LM), and vermis bilaterally. In addition, volumetric measurements of the cerebellum and its subregions were performed.Balance performance was significantly lower in individuals with BD compared to the control group (p < .05). In tractography analyses, a significant decrease in FA values was observed only in the SCP compared to the control group (p = .029). Volumetric analyses revealed a significant decrease in total cerebellar volume in the BB group (p < .05).These findings suggest that individuals with BB may exhibit impaired balance performance, particularly at the SCP level, along with reduced cerebellar volume and limited microstructural changes. While these results suggest a potential role for the cerebellum in the pathophysiology and balance-related mechanisms of BD, they need to be confirmed with a larger sample and longitudinal studies.

item.title: Longitudinal structural connectivity changes and cognitive trajectories in early multiple sclerosis: An exploratory graph-theory study.
item.description:
The neuroradiology journal
Multiple sclerosis (MS) is characterized by focal and diffuse white matter damage, often disrupting structural connectivity, and contributing to cognitive impairment. This exploratory study investigates early connectivity changes in MS and their relationship with cognition.In this longitudinal study, we recruited 18 early MS patients (31.92 ± 8.09 years, disease duration 0.91 ± 1.81 years, 10 females) and matched healthy controls (31.89 ± 8.15 years, 10 females) and acquired structural and diffusion-weighted MRI data at baseline and 10-month follow-up. Patients were categorized as cognitively preserved/recovered (CPR) or cognitively impaired/worsened (CIW) over time. Using graph-theory analysis, we measured network segregation, integration and centrality, and examined group and longitudinal differences.CPR and CIW patients showed distinct longitudinal connectivity patterns considering all nodes: CIW patients showed longitudinal increased segregation and centrality measures (increased strength, local efficiency and clustering coefficient, and decreased participation coefficient), while CPR patients had a longitudinal decrease in centrality and segregation metrics (decrease in strength, local efficiency and clustering coefficient, and increase in participation coefficient).Cognitive impairment is a predominant feature of MS, and might be closely related to structural connectivity changes, even in early MS. Understanding these early exploratory longitudinal associations between connectivity changes and cognition provides hypotheses for future larger studies on potential prevention of cognitive health in MS.

item.title: Frontal Low-Frequency Electroencephalographic Coherence in Bipolar Disorder: A Covariate-Controlled Secondary Analysis of a Public Resting-State EEG Feature Dataset.
item.description:
Clinical EEG and neuroscience
ObjectiveTo test whether bipolar disorder (BD) is associated with predefined frontal/frontopolar low-frequency scalp electroencephalography (EEG) coherence differences relative to healthy controls (HC), depressive disorder (DD), and schizophrenia (SZ) in a covariate-controlled reanalysis of a public resting-state EEG feature dataset.MethodsThe covariate-complete sample included 472 participants (93 HC, 66 BD, 196 DD, and 117 SZ). Analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) models adjusted for age, sex, education, and intelligence quotient (IQ). Primary outcomes were predefined frontal/frontopolar delta, theta, and combined delta-theta coherence means. Electrode-pair, regional, all-frequency, distributional, global-reference, frontopolar, and age sensitivity analyses assessed robustness.ResultsBD had higher adjusted coherence than all comparison groups across the three primary measures (partial η2 = .037-.040); Holm-adjusted BD-HC, BD-DD, and BD-SZ contrasts were significant for each measure. Features surviving false discovery rate correction were concentrated in the delta and theta bands. Findings were robust to distributional, outlier, and global-coherence analyses, but effects were strongest in frontopolar pairs and attenuated as anterior electrodes were excluded.ConclusionsBD showed higher covariate-adjusted frontal/frontopolar low-frequency scalp coherence than HC within this dataset. Differences from DD and SZ were smaller and concentrated in frontopolar pairs susceptible to ocular artifacts. Because only scalp-level coherence features were available and participant-level artifact-rejection data were unavailable, the findings do not establish a diagnostic biomarker, diagnostic specificity, or source-level mechanism. Artifact-controlled replication is required.

item.title: Cyclin-dependent kinase-like 5 (CDKL5) binds talin and is anchored at the postsynaptic density by direct PDZ interactions.
item.description:
Science advances
Cyclin-dependent kinase-like 5 (CDKL5) is a serine/threonine kinase essential for brain development and function. Mutations in CDKL5 cause CDKL5 deficiency disorder (CDD), a severe early-onset epileptic encephalopathy associated with impaired synapse formation and function. However, how CDKL5 mutations disrupt synaptic function remains unclear. Here, we show that the major neuronal isoform of CDKL5 contains a C-terminal PDZ domain-binding motif that mediates direct binding to PSD-95 and SHANK PDZ domains and recruits CDKL5 to the postsynaptic density. Disrupting this motif mislocalized CDKL5, reduced dendritic spine density, and impaired spine maturation. We also show that the CDKL5 kinase domain binds the R8 rod domain of the mechanosensitive scaffold talin. Mutation of the talin-binding interface or reduced cellular contractility altered CDKL5 positioning relative to focal adhesions. These findings define how CDKL5 is targeted to synapses, suggest that talin mechanoswitching may position CDKL5 kinase activity, and highlight the importance of C-terminal anchoring for interpreting pathogenic truncations.

item.title: Hidden Drowsiness in Wakefulness: Differences in Resting-State EEG Profiles in Natural Short Sleepers Versus Recommended Length Sleepers.
item.description:
Journal of sleep research
Chronic insufficient sleep affects cardiovascular, endocrine, immune and nervous systems and is linked to cognitive decline and increased mortality. Among habitual short sleepers, a subgroup known as natural short sleepers (NSS) report sleeping ≤ 6 h per night without experiencing subjective daytime dysfunction. However, discrepancies between subjective and objective markers of alertness raise questions about their true cognitive state. NSS have been described as high in behavioural activation, a phenotype overlapping with ADHD and mania in which dysregulation of resting-state brain arousal has been well documented. Despite these parallels, few studies have investigated the neurophysiological features of NSS. The current study examined resting-state EEG in NSS and recommended-length sleepers (RLS) during eyes-open conditions. Results showed that NSS exhibited significantly higher global alpha power and regionally steeper aperiodic exponents, particularly in occipital areas, both markers of increased drowsiness. Although global exponent values did not differ significantly, a significant Group × Region interaction was observed and NSS showed a trend toward increasing aperiodic exponents over time, suggesting less stable wakefulness under low-stimulation conditions. These findings point to subtle neurophysiological differences in NSS, raising the possibility that their perceived resilience to short sleep may mask underlying drowsiness.

item.title: Depressive symptoms moderate daily anticipated and momentary emotion dynamics and associate with complex brain network topology: Resting-state EEG and ecological momentary assessment evidence.
item.description:
Psychological medicine
Background The dynamic linkage between anticipated and momentary emotion is a core daily regulatory process, yet the psychopathological and neurophysiological mechanisms disrupting this linkage in depression remain unclear. By bridging macroscopic neural topology with microscopic behavioral dynamics, this study investigated the within-person dynamics of these emotions and their cross-level associations with depressive symptoms and brain network topology. Methods Integrating resting-state electroencephalography (rs-EEG) with a 14-day ecological momentary assessment (EMA; 3 assessments/day), we recruited 96 young adults. Minimum spanning tree (MST) analysis was applied to characterize baseline brain network topology across multiple frequency bands. Dynamic structural equation modeling (DSEM) was employed to examine within-person dynamics and cross-level statistical moderation. Results Anticipated emotion prospectively predicted subsequent momentary positive emotion (β = .191) and inversely predicted momentary negative emotion (β = -.125). However, baseline depressive symptoms significantly moderated this prospective affective dynamic: Johnson-Neyman analyses identified empirical transition ranges (PHQ-9 scores 5.7-9.7; mild symptom range) beyond which the prospective emotional link attenuated to non-significance. Furthermore, topological metrics in the theta and delta bands exhibited indirect statistical associations with daily emotional dynamics via their cross-sectional relationship with baseline depressive symptoms. Conclusions An attenuated prospective association between positive anticipation and subsequent momentary emotional experience represents a key affective alteration in depressive distress. This daily emotional attenuation co-occurs with elevated depressive distress and is indirectly associated with a centralized topological organization in low-frequency resting-state brain networks. These findings provide novel neurophysiological indicators and highlight the critical window for ecological interventions before symptom severity reaches the moderate range.

item.title: Volume of the mammillary bodies and cognitive trajectories in preclinical Alzheimer's disease.
item.description:
EBioMedicine
Background As part of the Papez circuit, the mammillary bodies (MB) play a key role in episodic memory, but their contribution to cognitive changes in preclinical Alzheimer's disease (AD) remains underexplored. Here, we investigated the associations between MB volume and cognitive decline in cognitively unimpaired older individuals, and whether these associations differed by Aβ status. Methods We examined 228 cognitively unimpaired older participants from the Harvard Ageing Brain Study (mean age: 73.5 ± 8.0, 64% female, all CDR = 0) who underwent baseline MRI, 11 C-Pittsburgh Compound B (PiB) PET imaging and annual cognitive assessments. MB volume was quantified using the FastSurfer-HypVINN tool, and PiB status was derived from a neocortical aggregate. Cognition was assessed over up to 11 years using the Preclinical Alzheimer's Cognitive Composite 5 (PACC5), as well as a memory and executive function composite. Findings At baseline, PiB+ participants with lower MB volume showed poorer cognitive performance on the PACC5 and on memory and executive function composites. Longitudinally, lower baseline MB volume was associated with steeper memory and PACC5 decline, particularly among PiB+ participants. Control analyses showed that associations between posterior hypothalamic volume and cognitive performance, at baseline and over time, did not differ by PiB status. Similarly, associations between hippocampal volume and baseline cognition did not differ by PiB status, but hippocampal volume was associated with cognitive decline, more strongly in PiB+ individuals. Interpretation These findings indicate that lower MB volume was associated with poorer cognitive performance and steeper decline in PiB+ individuals, suggesting that MB volume may serve as an indicator of cognitive decline in preclinical AD. Funding National Institutes of Health, Alzheimer's Association.

item.title: Postoperative delirium is associated with accelerated brain ageing: an exploratory cohort study.
item.description:
British journal of anaesthesia
Background Advanced age is a major risk factor for both delirium and dementia. A potential early biomarker for dementia is the brain-predicted age difference (brainPAD). We hypothesised that brain ageing accelerates after postoperative delirium (POD), and that increased brainPAD is associated with cognitive decline. Methods Brain MRI scans were obtained in 287 older patients before and 3 months after major elective surgery, and two MRI scans at similar time intervals were obtained in 46 nonsurgical control participants. We computed grey matter brainPAD in patients with POD (POD+), patients without POD (POD-), and nonsurgical controls. The Trail Making Test (TMT) was administered at both time points to examine associations between changes in brainPAD and changes in attention/processing speed (TMT-A) and executive task switching (TMT-B and TMT B-A). Results Compared with the POD- group, brainPAD increased by an additional 6 (sd=3) months over time in the POD+ group (P=0.002). For each 1 year-over-year increase in brain age gap, patients took 2.3 s longer to complete the TMT-A (P=0.016), whereas no association was observed with TMT-B (P=0.254) or TMT B-A (P=0.91). Conclusions Postoperativ edelirium is associated with accelerated brain ageing, which in turn is associated with decline in attention and processing speed. These findings help to understand the complex relationship between ageing, delirium, and dementia. Clinical trial registration NCT02265263.

item.title: Speech and music organize neural activity differently over time in human superior temporal cortex
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Speech and music engage overlapping auditory cortex. We asked whether they shape the timing of local activity in ways that regional response strength alone leaves unresolved. In intracranial recordings from 30 participants watching a film with alternating music and speech, 1-10-Hz activity in the superior temporal gyrus (STG) had higher sample entropy during music, indicating that similar short patterns were less likely to persist (mean paired difference = 0.02256, FDR q = 0.00753). The contrast persisted in comparisons of adjacent film blocks and was larger relative to surrogate signals matched for amplitude distribution and approximate power spectrum. Speech elicited higher STG high-frequency power in the intracranial subset and stronger bilateral STG BOLD responses in all 30 participants in the separately acquired fMRI recordings. Together, these findings show that the soundtrack category associated with stronger regional responses differs from the one associated with greater local temporal irregularity. The temporal organisation of local activity therefore adds a dimension to how shared auditory cortex responds to natural sounds.

item.title: The information architecture of the naturalistic human brain
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
How does the brain orchestrate its central currency, information, for complex adaptive cognition in the real world? Here we provide a comprehensive investigation into the spatiotemporal structure of qualitatively distinct modes of information dynamics in the human brain under ecological conditions. Applying a novel framework for information decomposition to fMRI data from individuals watching full-length feature films, we reveal a multidimensional large-scale information architecture, wherein different schemes for storing, transferring, and transforming representations occupy disjoint topographic and network profiles. Further, this architecture reveals a computational division of labour, with certain regions acting as generalists that support multiple information-processing schemes and others specialising in a few. We show how these interactions reconfigure over time, coalescing into a structured cycle synchronised by sensory input, whose elements are tuned to semantic kinematics. Finally, we replicate these findings in an independent, large-scale dataset. Together, we provide a formal and empirical foundation for understanding the principles that govern distributed computation in the human brain during everyday life.

item.title: Rage bait: a neurofunctional signature of moral outrage elicited by social media
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Moral outrage is ubiquitous online, with powerful emotional and motivational consequences for social life. Combining naturalistic fMRI during exposure to short-form social-media videos depicting moral violations with predictive modeling, we developed a neurofunctional signature of subjective moral outrage (MONS) in discovery/validation (n=80/30) cohorts. MONS predicted experienced outrage and punishment tendencies across cohorts. Positive predictive weights encompassed regions implicated in mentalizing, threat detection and action initiation (precuneus, posterior cingulate, periaqueductal gray, hypothalamus, cerebellum), whereas negative weights involved valuation and behavioral flexibility systems (amygdala, orbitofrontal cortex). Across 11 datasets (n=478), MONS captured anger and disgust but was dissociable from general negative affect and affective arousal. Notably, MONS did not predict perceived moral wrongness in conventional moral judgment paradigms, suggesting that moral outrage is not reducible to more cognitive moral evaluation. Findings provide a moral outrage neurofunctional model that delineates its relationship to other affective states and distinguishes it from traditional moral judgment.

item.title: Distinct Relaxation Kurtosis Imaging-Derived White Matter Microstructural Phenotypes Tracking Alzheimer's Disease Pathology and Cognitive Decline
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
White matter (WM) pathology is increasingly recognized as an early, mechanistically relevant feature of Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet sensitive in-vivo biomarkers remain limited. Here, we introduce an MRI-based Relaxation Kurtosis Imaging (RKI) technique sensitive to WM microstructure. RKI metrics differentiate two distinct phenotypes of white matter that follow divergent microstructural trajectories in preclinical and early symptomatic AD. We examined their relationships to AD progression, gray matter (GM) pathology, and clinical impairment in 305 adults spanning amyloid-negative to amyloid-positive stages with normal cognition, preclinical AD, and early symptomatic AD. Pathological changes in one phenotype reflected axonal alterations without myelin loss and were anatomically coupled to GM cortical pathology, strengthening with disease stage - a signature of Wallerian degeneration. Alterations in the other phenotype represented WM demyelination. A model incorporating RKI-metrics, age, sex, amyloid status, APOE genotype, and brain volume classified Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR)-based impairment with an area under the receiver operating curve (AUC) = 0.933, with the RKI-metrics contributing 27% (second only to amyloid at 40%). While both phenotypes related comparably to concurrent cognition (each ~27%), the "axonal" phenotype showed the strongest relationship to subsequent cognitive decline (41% of explained variance), with the "myelin" phenotype contributing 31%. These RKI-defined dual white matter phenotypes provide new insight into AD pathology, adding diagnostic and prognostic value for tracking both current cognitive status and future cognitive decline.

item.title: Is Latin American brain anatomy "normal"? Construction and evaluation of a Chilean brain template
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Many neuroimaging processes use a brain reference anatomical template; the most widely used is the Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) template. Yet studies have shown that different populations exhibit different global brain features, and the use of a unique Canadian template may introduce biases in analyses for other populations. The purpose of this work is to construct a brain template that accurately represents our local population in Chile. In addition, our project explicitly addresses another pressing challenge: the limited availability of high-field MR scanners in Latin America. In this context, we will build our template using a 0.55T MR scanner, thus ensuring not only population specificity but also methodological alignment with the technological realities of our healthcare systems. Healthy volunteers (n = 76, ages 18–60) underwent T1-weighted MRI. Images were preprocessed and iteratively registered via rigid and non-linear steps to generate a Chilean template (CL76). Evaluation involved dimensional comparisons with Canadian, Indian, Chinese, and Korean templates. Deformation metrics were estimated for an additional 23 volunteers. The Chilean template measures 166 × 132 × 100 mm3, smaller than the Canadian one (179 × 137 × 118 mm3), and has distinct proportions, particularly the width/height ratio of 1.31 versus 1.16. Deformation of a test population onto CL76 was significantly lower (p = 0.010) and less variable than that of MNI152. The top deformed regions onto CL76 or onto MNI152 differed, confirming population specificity on the template. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first brain template generated in South America; however, we do not claim to represent the entire continent—only a specific population from Chile. This work highlights the need for broader representation across diverse populations, particularly to counterbalance the current over-representation of individuals from high-income countries with established research and imaging infrastructures.

item.title: Data-Driven Decomposition of Precisely Aligned Fiber-Orientation-Preserving Probabilistic Tractography Connectomes with Non-Negative Matrix Factorization
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
The major goals of the Human Connectome Project (HCP) were to characterize the structural and functional connectivity of the human brain. Although there has been tremendous work done for functional connectivity, including application of a variety of data driven decomposition approaches, structural connectivity from the HCP has seen less attention. This work presents a collection of methodological advances that, in combination, enable similar approaches to be applied to diffusion tractography data. Here, we use multi-modal non-linear volumetric alignment with FSL's MultiMOdal Registration Framework (MMORF) to precisely align white matter tracts and globular gray matter nuclei, use the White matter Hierarchical Modelling (WHIM) method to align voxel-wise fiber orientations, enable efficient GPU-accelerated computation and storage of full resolution probabilistic gray matter x white matter x fiber sparse tractography matrices in precise alignment across individuals using the aforementioned MMORF and WHIM alignments together with areal-feature-based cortical surface registration. These tractography dense connectomes can be averaged across individuals and sparse, computationally efficient non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) can be applied to perform data-driven decompositions into white matter tracts and gray matter projection territories. The primary outputs of this effort to date are 1) A set of HCP software pipelines enabling such analyses, 2) A new unbiased HCP-derived volumetric standard space that is representative of the young adult brain and follows ACPC orientation conventions across individuals. 3) Reproducible NMF decompositions of HCP young adult tractography data into white matter tracts and gray matter projection territories, which could be projected using non-negative dual regression back to individuals. These data represent a starting point for a new generation of data-driven atlasing efforts for human white matter, and these methods can be applied to study the white matter in development, aging, and brain diseases.

item.title: Modelling vortex interactions reveals distinct patterns of brain reconfiguration following psilocybin and escitalopram
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Major depressive disorder is a leading cause of disability, yet how interventions reorganise brain dynamics remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated how psilocybin and escitalopram reshape brain dynamics in depression using pre- and post-treatment resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) from a double-blind randomised controlled trial ( NCT03429075 ). We compared two whole-brain modelling approaches: conventional signal-space modelling describing interactions between regional brain signals, and vortex-space modelling capturing interactions between evolving patterns of local synchronisation. This represents the first application of vortex-space modelling to a psychiatric disorder. Vortex space was more sensitive than signal space in most analyses, including distinguishing treatment-related brain states, relating baseline connectivity to clinical improvement and predicting response to escitalopram. Our results further revealed distinct patterns of reorganisation following the two interventions. Psilocybin produced widespread increases in vortex-space effective connectivity and reduced network modularity, whereas escitalopram showed no comparable changes. Despite these differences, greater increases in brain turbulence (i.e., spatiotemporal variability in local synchronisation) were associated with greater symptom reduction in both treatments, with a significant post-treatment increase in responders. These findings suggest that psilocybin and escitalopram may reorganise brain dynamics in markedly different ways and yet share dynamical features associated with clinical improvement. Overall, vortex-space modelling offers a promising framework for characterising brain dynamics in depression and its successful treatment.

item.title: The Dual Nature of Syntactic Node Count: Facilitating and Inhibiting Sentence Comprehension
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Neurolinguistic research on syntactic processing has used Node Count, the number of syntactic nodes assumed to be built at each word, to investigate how structure-building effort affects brain activity. However, several recent studies cast doubt on the presumed link between Node Count and processing effort; they observe negative correlations between Node Count and reading times. These facilitatory effects raise an alternative hypothesis: rather than reflecting structure-building effort, Node Count may index structure-mediated predictability. To test this hypothesis, we first relate Node Count to an information-theoretic measure of contextual support, the pointwise mutual information (PMI) between a word and its context. We then evaluate the relationship between Node Count and reading times from three large-scale naturalistic English datasets. For these analyses, we derive Node Count under three grammar formalisms (phrase-structure grammar, dependency grammar, and combinatory categorial grammar) and multiple parsing strategies. Variants whose count reflects integrative parsing steps correlate positively with PMI and show a dual behavioral profile: robust facilitation in immediate regions, consistent with structure-mediated predictability, and a delayed slowdown in spillover regions, most consistent with the cost of contextual semantic integration. The facilitatory effect explains reading-time variance beyond GPT-2 surprisal, indicating that Node Count has unique psycholinguistic value as an index of human prediction. These results highlight the role of structural representations in human language processing and underscore the need for a careful interpretation of the observed correlations between Node Count and brain activity in neurolinguistic studies.

item.title: Cerebellum–white-matter proportionality is associated with cognition but not explained by lobular anatomy
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Background. A previously identified association between whole-cerebellum and cerebral-white-matter (Cer:WM) allocation and cognitive ability does not establish a lobular mechanism. We tested whether this association in Amsterdam Open MRI Collection (AOMIC) ID1000 was robust to a new cerebellar measurement and explained by regional allocation. Methods. First-run T1-weighted scans from 928 participants were processed outcome-blind with FastSurfer/CerebNet v2.6.0. Before regional measurements were joined to cognition, the primary exposure was fixed as the log ratio of bilateral Crus I, Crus II and VIIb to bilateral lobules I-IV and V. Blinded quality control produced one anatomical exclusion; final analyses used 925 participants and adjusted for age, sex, tissue scale and five-part macroanatomical composition. Results. The newly measured Cer:WM association remained positive (standardized β = 0.101, 95% CI 0.029–0.174, p=.0063; old/new cerebellar totals r=.982). The locked posterior:anterior ratio was null (β = 0.004, 95% CI -0.059-0.067, p=.908); its confidence interval excluded standardized effects of magnitude ≥ 0.067, and a post-hoc equivalence test supported equivalence within ± 0.10 (TOST p=.0014). The regional term attenuated the baseline macro Cer:WM coefficient by only 0.28%. Global lobular-composition and asymmetry tests were null, and regional augmentation was uninformative in cross-validation. Conclusions. The AOMIC Cer:WM association is robust to cerebellar measurement method but is not explained by detectable lobular allocation in healthy young adults. Cerebral white matter and cerebellum showed markedly different intracranial-volume scaling (exponents 0.606 versus 0.372), underscoring allometric and compositional specification as an important benchmark for cerebellar morphometry.

item.title: Diffusion tractography of the olfactory pathway and odor recognition
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Olfactory processing constitutes a unique system where sensory input is directly linked to integrative perceptual processing, providing an optimal model for investigating how perceptual input is transformed into higher-order functions. However, the neural substrates of olfaction remain incompletely understood. Here, we delineated central olfactory pathways using advanced tractography and examined associations between tractography metrics and olfactory functions. We acquired T1-weighted and diffusion-weighted images from 129 healthy participants and assessed olfactory function in 59 individuals using a T&T olfactometer. We defined the primary olfactory cortex and secondary olfactory structures and their connections. White matter query language was used to extract central olfactory pathways from refined whole-brain tractography according to neuroanatomical rules. We analyzed the number of streamlines and the laterality index of these pathways in relation to olfactory detection and recognition thresholds. For the total olfactory fascicle, more streamlines were observed in the left than the right hemisphere, and greater leftward lateralization was significantly associated with lower mean recognition thresholds. In conclusion, we successfully reconstructed central olfactory pathways beyond the primary olfactory cortex and provided evidence supporting the neural basis of higher-order olfactory functions. Leftward lateralization may enhance associative olfactory processing by reducing circuit redundancy and allocating additional neural capacity.

item.title: Correspondence Between Structural and Functional Connectivity Within White Matter
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract White matter functional networks (WMFNs) derived from resting-state BOLD fluctuations have been identified across multiple datasets, but whether they correspond to coherent anatomical units defined by the underlying axonal architecture remains untested. Here we tested WM structural connectivity-functional connectivity (SC-FC) coupling directly by asking whether regions co-assigned to the same WMFN are preferentially linked by WM tracts. Using resting-state fMRI and diffusion MRI from the Human Connectome Project 7T dataset (N = 161), we derived 11 WMFNs per session (after exclusion of one boundary network) via k-means clustering of voxel-level functional connectivity (FC), constructed structural connectivity (SC) using multi-shell multi-tissue constrained spherical deconvolution with anatomically constrained tractography, and quantified the correlation between SC and FC across within- and between-network edges. Within-network coupling was two to three times higher than between-network coupling in both sessions (Session 1: r within = 0.59 vs. r between = 0.20; Session 2: r within = 0.66 vs. r between = 0.28; p < 0.001). The increased coupling was also observed across subjects, in terms of survived matching of edge counts, and disappeared when network labels were permuted. Network-level coupling was heterogeneous and concentrated in projection pathways spanning the midbrain and medulla oblongata, with rank ordering of the six highest-coupling networks identical across sessions. These findings provide structural support that WMFNs are coherent anatomical-functional units and support reconceptualising WM as a structured contributor to the brain's functional architecture rather than a passive transmission medium.

item.title: Beyond the Group Average: Interindividual Variability in Neural Activity During Written Word Processing
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract The processing of language and reading has been a subject of interest for neuropsychologists for many decades. Nevertheless, variability between subjects within the language network has received comparatively little attention. In this study, we employed a precision fMRI approach to examine between-subject variability in neural activity during single-word reading. In order to assess the similarity between subjects' activation patterns, two methods were utilised: Spearman's rank correlation and the Jaccard index. Following this, an exploratory correlation was performed between the similarity and subjects' characteristics. As part of the quantification of between-subject variance, the brain regions characterised by the most variance were identified using interclass correlation coefficients (ICC). The participants exhibited a moderate similarity in their activation patterns, which was correlated with their reading performance and psychopathological traits. Brain regions exhibiting notably high interindividual variability were predominantly located within or adjacent to the language network, suggesting variability in the precise location and extent of the language network among subjects. A comparison of the group-level activation map derived from the same sample revealed that it provided only a moderate representation of the individual maps. The findings underscore the significance of integrating group-level analyses with individual-centred methodologies to achieve more precise characterisation of the neural organisation of language and advance our understanding of the brain-behaviour relation.

item.title: Attention increases the spread of modality-invariant information across the cortex.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Attention shapes our perception by allowing us to focus on relevant stimuli that are selected for conscious processing. In this work we assessed to what degree attention influences the extraction of modality-invariant information, that is, information that is independent of the input stimulus modality. To this end, we analyze fMRI data of subjects viewing naturalistic images and reading short textual descriptions while paying attention to only one of the two modalities. Using cross-modality decoding, we found modality-invariant representations in a small area of the cortex even in the absence of attention, spreading to much larger regions when stimuli are attended. This work demonstrates how state-of-the-art decoding techniques on large-scale data can be used to expand our knowledge on how attention shapes specific high-level representations in the brain.
